notes.byline: The SCFL NewsRoom · The Player Desk
notes.headline: Three Names On The Wire, And One Of Them Is Real
notes.dek: Every roster place in this league is taken but eight. Of everyone left, exactly one has a share that has gone up every week he has played.
notes.method: Who is owned comes from this morning's roster pull — all sixteen teams, starters, bench and reserve — matched on the NFL's player id first and on the name second, because the pool contains two K.Colemans and only the id separates them. Usage is counted out of nflverse play-by-play: a player's carries plus targets against his own team's carries plus pass attempts, week by week. Ages are floored from birth dates, not rounded; rounding made three of these men a year older than they are.

x.n: of 16; six teams had not played

body.x: The first thing to say about the waiver wire in a 16-team league with 21 places a roster is that there is almost nothing on it. Three hundred and twenty-eight of the three hundred and thirty-six places are filled. Across five weeks, twenty unrostered players at any skill position have had as many as twelve touches between them, and most of those twenty are backup tight ends and third receivers whose usage is going nowhere.
So the question is not who is good. It is who is being used more this week than last, and whether he is young enough to matter next year.

body.x: Kimani Vidal is the claim

He is the only unrostered player in the league whose share has risen every week he has been used: nothing, nothing, 6 per cent, 12, 17. Twenty-two touches, 112 receiving yards and two touchdowns out of a role that did not exist in September. At 25 he is not a long-term asset, but he is the one name on this list where the offence is visibly handing him more.

x: Omarion Hampton is not hurt. He took fourteen carries in week five, the same week Vidal took ten touches, and he has seventy-nine for the season. Vidal is the third man in a three-man backfield who happens to be the one gaining.
That is a bench stash, not a starter. It is still the best thing available.

body.x: Kevin Coleman Jr. is the one to buy before the price

Twenty-three, a rookie, and his targets have gone 2, none, 4, 4, 7. Eleven per cent of Miami's throws in each of the last two weeks, up from four. And he has 36 yards on five catches, which is to say nothing has actually happened yet.
Nothing has happened yet. That is the entire argument for picking him up.

That is the point. The desk's own rule is that a rising share with no production is the buy and a flat share with touchdowns on top is the trap, and this is the first half of it. For a roster rebuilding toward next season he is free, he is 23, and the only thing he costs is a bench place.
Dameon Pierce is not a keeper. He is a trade.

Pierce had no touches at all in the first four weeks and sixteen in week five, 28 per cent of everything Philadelphia ran or threw. Saquon Barkley and Tank Bigsby had none between them in that game. Whatever the reason, the job was his for an afternoon.

He is 26, which puts him outside every reason this roster is holding anything. But a free running back with a starter's workload has real value to a team trying to win this season, and the way to use him is to claim him and sell him while the workload lasts — not to hold him and find out.
And the ones to leave

x: Darnell Washington has the best raw line here — 11 catches, 131 yards, a touchdown — and plays the position this desk measured at 6.8 points a start, below the kicker. In non-PPR that line is about 19 points across five games, under four a week, and his share went down in week five.
Corey Kiner went 9, 4, 12, nothing, 11 per cent. That is not a trend, it is a weather pattern.
Bryce Lance sits at 7 per cent behind a receiver this desk already flagged as New Orleans' most-used man. There is no room in front of him.
Darren Waller is rising and is 34, which is somebody else's problem.

body.k: One caveat with a date on it
x: This was built with thirteen of week five's sixteen games counted. Atlanta, Baltimore, Buffalo, Carolina, Kansas City and the Rams had not played. Anybody who breaks out tonight or tomorrow is not on this page, and the board is rebuilt from the same two files the moment they have.

notes.byline: The SCFL NewsRoom · The Trade Desk
notes.headline: What A Second-Round Pick Is Actually Worth
notes.dek: Not much, and the league's own value chart has been saying so the whole time. The entire second round is worth less than the top two picks put together.
notes.method: Every figure is read straight off the two calibrated numbers the league already keeps: the pickValueChart in draft-intel.json (pick 1 = 1000 points, dollars = points over ten) and the priceGuide in the same file, which is calibrated to 235 real SCFL trades across six years.

body.x: This one started as a correction. The desk had been pricing second-round picks like real capital in trade talk, and got told flatly that a mid-second could not possibly be worth that much. It isn't. The league's own chart has been saying so since it was built, and nobody had read it out loud.
The arithmetic

The chart puts the 1.01 at 1,000 points and runs down to 45 at the 32nd and last pick. Dollars are points over ten, so the first pick is $100. The 24th pick — the middle of the second round, the thing people mean when they say “a mid-second” — is 100 points. Ten dollars. One tenth of the top pick.

Averaged across its sixteen picks, the whole second round comes to 99.7 points a pick: call it ten dollars for any second you cannot place. And added together, all sixteen second-rounders are worth 1,595 points — less than picks one and two on their own, which are 1,860.
The entire second round is worth less than the top two picks.
So why does one cost fifteen dollars?

Because that is what the market charges. The price guide, calibrated to 235 real trades in this league, puts a future second at $15 — and $15 on this chart is 150 points, which is the 19th pick. The third selection of the second round. Not the middle of it.

That gap is the whole lesson. Buying an unplaced future second costs about half again what the pick is likely to become. You are not paying for a player; you are paying for the option on one, and the option is dearer than the thing. Sellers of future seconds in this league are getting a good price, and buyers are paying a premium for the privilege of not knowing yet.

body.x: Where the desk went wrong

Two scales were in play and both of them put the 1.01 at $100, which is exactly why it was so easy to mix them up. DynastyProcess prices players on a superflex curve anchored at $100 for the 1.01. The league chart prices picks on a curve anchored at the same place but deliberately steeper and more top-heavy, because that is how managers here have actually traded for six years. Agreeing at the anchor is not the same as agreeing anywhere else, and the further down the board you go the further apart they get.

Quoting a player's DynastyProcess dollars against a pick's league-chart dollars therefore reads fine and is wrong, and it is wrong in a consistent direction: it makes picks look like real money. They are not. Below about pick 24 they are a rounding error with a round number attached.

x: A future 1st is $40 and a current mid-1st is about the same. A future 2nd is $15 but ought to be $10. Anything from pick 28 down is a sweetener you throw in, not a price you pay.
And there are only 32 of these in existence against 304 roster places, which is the other reason a second-round pick cannot buy a starter: the draft is not where this league's players come from.

notes.byline: The SCFL NewsRoom · The Trade Desk
notes.headline: The Warren File
notes.dek: He is twenty-seven for three more weeks, he is worth seven dollars, and his receiving role is the best it has ever been. All three of those are reasons to sell.
notes.method: Age is computed from the birth date in nflverse's players.csv, which is the NFL's own player table — not from a name search, which on an earlier pass in this league returned fathers instead of sons. Value is the August 2026 DynastyProcess snapshot. Target share is counted out of nflverse play-by-play, weeks one to five.

x.n: 27, and 28 on the first of November
week five, his highest of the year

body.x: The question was whether Jaylen Warren is worth seven dollars or seventy. Seven. The August snapshot has him at $7 on the scale where the 1.01 is $100, and the five years of snapshots behind it tell the story of why: nothing in 2022, $2 in 2023, a peak of $12 in 2024, back to $3 in 2025, and $7 now. He has been bouncing around the same small number for half a decade.
The case for keeping him

It is not nothing. His share of Pittsburgh's passing work has climbed almost every week of this season — 15 per cent, 10, 12, 17, 19 — and 27 targets through five weeks for 230 yards is a genuine receiving back's usage, not a change-of-pace back's. In a non-PPR league that is worth less than it looks, but it is real, and it is the best his role has been.
The case against

He turns 28 on the first of November. This roster is rebuilding for next year and does not need wins this one, which makes a 27-year-old running back with a $7 price the single least useful kind of asset to be holding: too old to appreciate, too cheap to headline a deal, and good enough right now that somebody else will want him.
Too old to appreciate, too cheap to headline a deal, and good enough right now that somebody else wants him.
What he can actually fetch

Seven dollars does not buy a future second at its market price of $15, which is why every version of this trade came back as a bundle rather than a straight swap. It does buy roughly a mid-second ($10) at a small premium, and it buys a young receiver the market has not priced yet. Both of those are better things for this roster to own in October 2026 than a running back who will be 28 by Thanksgiving.

x: Rebuilding for next year. Wins this season are not the point, so age is the first filter on anything coming back and the first argument for anything going out.

notes.byline: The SCFL NewsRoom · The Player Desk
notes.headline: Target Share Is The Signal
notes.dek: Fantasy points tell you what already happened. Share of the targets tells you whether it will happen again. The desk said so and then immediately ignored it.
notes.method: Target share is a player's targets divided by his own team's pass attempts that week, counted directly out of nflverse play-by-play for weeks one to five and matched on the NFL's player id rather than on an abbreviated name. Sacks are excluded; a sack is not a target.

body.x: The rule the desk went in with: when you are deciding whether a waiver pickup is real, fantasy points are the worst available evidence. Two touchdowns in a quiet month will outscore eight honest targets a week, and only one of those repeats. Share of his own team's throws is the signal, because it is a measure of what the offence intends rather than of what bounced in.
Then the desk recommended a receiver on the strength of his fantasy points. Here is the table it should have run first.

body.x: The correction, in public

Josh Cameron was recommended here on the back of two touchdowns. His share across the first four weeks was 9, 0, 7 and 8 per cent — flat, small, and exactly the profile the rule exists to catch. Twelve targets in five games is not a role. The touchdowns were the reason to look and not the reason to buy.

Week five is the first thing in his file that argues the other way: six targets out of thirty-nine, 15 per cent, nearly double anything before it. One week is one week. But it is the right kind of week, and it is the number to watch rather than the yards.
The touchdowns were the reason to look. They were not the reason to buy.
What the table says that the points do not

x: Devaughn Vele is the most-used player on the list and the market has him at nothing. A 24 per cent share in week five, rising almost every week, 37 targets through five games — and a dynasty value of zero dollars. He is also 28, which is the catch: that usage is a win-now asset, and a roster rebuilding for next year is buying the wrong year of him.
Michael Pittman is being used like a fourth receiver. Twelve targets, two separate weeks at zero per cent, no touchdowns. There was never a version of this where he helped.

Mumpfield has one good week and nothing around it. Eight targets in week three is 15 per cent; either side of it is four and six. That is a spike, not a trend, and a bye week means there is nothing new to read.

Loveland's share is the real thing on this list. It has climbed from 7 to 12 per cent with a 26 per cent week in the middle of it — which is why the market has him at $43 and rising while his box score says 110 yards and no touchdowns.

body.k: The rule, written down so it gets followed
x: Before recommending anybody off waivers: look up his share of his own team's throws, week by week, and look at the shape of it. A flat small number with touchdowns on top is noise. A rising number with nothing on top is the buy.
Then check the age against the plan. A rising share on a 28-year-old is somebody else's asset.

notes.byline: The SCFL NewsRoom · The Player Desk
notes.headline: A Tight End Scores Less Than Your Kicker
notes.dek: In a non-PPR league the tight end slot is the cheapest seat in the lineup. Which is an argument for selling one, and the reason the one worth selling is the one you keep.
notes.method: Every starter's points for weeks one to four of 2026, taken from the committed week files rather than from a live fetch, and grouped by the slot the manager actually started him in. Week five is left out because its file was pulled while the week was still being played.

body.x: The premise offered to the desk was that tight ends do not score a lot. In this league, in this format, that is not an opinion. It is the lowest number on the board.

head: Slot
Average
Median
Top tenth
Starts
body.cap: Points per start by slot, weeks one to four of 2026, all sixteen teams. Non-PPR, so the tight end's catches pay nothing on their own.

body.x: The average started tight end in this league is worth two and a half points a week less than the average kicker.

It is not only the average. The ceiling is low too: a top-tenth week from a tight end is 15.5 points, which is less than a top-tenth week from the defence and barely two thirds of what a running back's good week pays. And the gap between a very good tight end and an ordinary one is about ten points a week, against fifteen at running back and twelve at quarterback. The slot compresses everybody into the same small range.
So sell the tight end

That is the obvious conclusion and it is the one the desk reached, and it needs one correction before it is safe to act on. The tight end on this roster worth selling is Colston Loveland, who is 22, whose target share has climbed from 7 to 12 per cent with a 26 per cent week in the middle of it, and whom the market has repriced from $21 to $43 in a year.

Everything in that sentence except the position argues for keeping him. He is the right age for a roster rebuilding toward next season, he is the only asset in the group whose price is going up, and his 110 yards and no touchdowns through five weeks mean his value is entirely in what the market believes rather than in what he has produced — which is the definition of an asset you sell high or hold, not one you dump for convenience.

x: The position being cheap is an argument for not paying for tight ends. It is not an argument for giving one away at a discount, and a mid-second (ten dollars) against a $43 asset is a discount.
If Loveland goes, he goes for something that moves the rebuild forward — a real pick or a young receiver with a share — and the second tight end is the one that leaves for a sweetener.
